policy_title: Support marriage through the tax system
stated: Reform UK will introduce a UK 25% transferable marriage tax allowance as soon as finances allow, meaning no tax on the first £25,000 of income for either spouse, to make work pay and incentivise people back into the workplace.

source.quote: Support Marriage Through the Tax System As soon as finances allow, introduce a UK 25% transferable marriage tax allowance. This would mean no tax on the first £25,000 of income for either spouse. This will help make work pay and incentivise people trapped on benefits back into the workplace.

bearing_set.reason: Raising the effective personal allowance to £25,000 and making it transferable between spouses directly increases household disposable income for married couples, a non-negligible effect on affordability of essentials.

The policy explicitly targets work incentives; however, transferable allowances have a contested and potentially negative effect on secondary-earner (usually female) labour-market participation, making the employment-incentive claim genuinely contested and non-negligible.
Directly raises the tax-free allowance to £25,000 per spouse for married couples, materially reducing household tax burden and increasing take-home pay — a concrete move on the key O11 indicators.

Raising the personal allowance from ~£12,570 to £25,000 for all married couples would cost many billions in foregone revenue; no specific funding mechanism is stated, materially moving the funded-vs-borrowed balance and debt-path sustainability indicators.

Benefit accrues exclusively to married couples (not cohabiting, single parents, or civil-partnership households in unclear scope), and within that group is larger in absolute terms for higher earners — concrete distributional incidence that widens the gap between household types and across the income distribution.

membership_note: Three fundamentals earn real verdicts: O11 (clear tax-relief benefit), O12 (large unfunded revenue cost), and O14 (regressive and marriage-status-restricted distributional incidence). The stated labour-supply rationale ('incentivise people back into the workplace') is too uncertain in direction and magnitude to earn a non-negligible verdict on O13 at the aggregate level.
